source: Sinha et al. (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE
finding: Best reasoning models create a valid counterexample for under 9 percent of subtly wrong competition solutions, though they could solve up to about half of the same problems.
numbers: 324 samples (from 647 Codeforces problems, 304 authors). o3-mini (high) with code execution < 9 percent; Elo-based estimate of solving 48.7 percent (R1: rating 2029, 44.0 percent).
quote: even o3-mini (high) with code execution feedback, can create counterexamples for only < 9% of incorrect solutions
limits: Only code-checkable claims (algorithm problems, C++ mostly: 317 of 324). Solve rate is estimated from ratings, not measured.
agent_relevance: Finding a counterexample can be harder than solving. Do not trust a free-text 'find a counterexample' call; ground it in code that runs both rules.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE: giving the correct solution
finding: Showing the model the correct solution did not close the gap. Knowing the right answer is not enough to find where a wrong rule fails.
numbers: Table 1, 'w/ Correct' column: best models stay under about 10 percent (R1 and o3-mini in the 9 percent range); gains over zero-shot were small.
limits: Table cells read from a garbled PDF-to-text layout; check the paper before quoting single cells.
agent_relevance: The S7 discriminating test needs a search procedure, not only a reference rule. A second candidate rule in hand is not enough.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE: execution feedback and few-shot
finding: A ReAct agent with up to 10 code runs mostly did not raise counterexample success. Execution feedback did remove invalid-input errors. Few-shot expert rationales helped Gemini but gave little or hurt others.
numbers: R1 and V3 had 0 validation failures with the agent, versus 45 and 36 in zero-shot. Only R1 showed modest gains from execution.
limits: Single benchmark; small cell sizes (about 3 to 9 percent of 324).
agent_relevance: Running code fixes format errors but not the idea of where to look. Use code for checking inputs, not for inventing the discriminating input.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE: forced random search
finding: Models rarely chose a search strategy on their own. When told to write a random input generator plus a brute-force checker, reasoning models did not improve much, but o3-mini doubled and found different cases.
numbers: RandSearch success: V3 4.0, Flash Thinking 3.7, R1 4.0, o3-mini (high) 8.3 percent. About 35 percent of runs ended with an invalid counterexample; 86 percent of those came from wrong brute-force code, 14 percent from validation errors. o3-mini RandSearch cracked 6 percent new submissions that other strategies missed (3 percent new with the oracle correct solution).
limits: 2-minute search cap. Brute-force code written by the same model is itself unreliable.
agent_relevance: Random search plus a brute-force oracle is complementary to reasoning; but the oracle must be trusted code. Use as a second method inside S7, not a replacement.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE: what predicts success
finding: Counterexample success was not predicted by problem difficulty, author expertise, or how many tests the wrong code passed.
numbers: No clear trend across five percentile buckets for R1 and o3-mini (all strategies pooled). Median tests passed by the wrong code: 17. Random-test filter removed 58 of 403 (14 percent) as too easy; 21 (6 percent) bait submissions removed.
limits: No trend does not mean no cause; buckets were coarse.
agent_relevance: Cannot decide from problem difficulty when to spend on a counterexample search. Use a fixed cheap trigger (two rules still fit) instead.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify
finding: Eleven LLMs repeat the Wason 2-4-6 error: they mostly propose tests that fit their own guess. Success is low and rises with more tests that break the current guess.
numbers: 11 LLMs, task success 6 percent to 78 percent within 45 turns; synthetic hidden rules; I:C ratio (incompatible to compatible tests) correlates positively with success in both thinking and non-thinking models (80 episodes per cell).
limits: Number-triple game only; one prompt style; I:C is a proxy for falsifying intent. Preprint.
agent_relevance: S7: a model left alone will pick confirming tests. Force one test whose outcome differs between the leading rules.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: instructions that work
finding: Two human debiasing prompts help. Think-in-Opposites (build a test opposite on one property of the last test) raised success in every model setting; Dual-Goal (label outcomes DAX and MED) in 8 of 11.
numbers: Average success 42 to 56 percent. Qwen3-8B thinking 0.21 to 0.36, Qwen3-32B thinking 0.41 to 0.61, Gemini-2.5-Pro 0.73 to 0.78 (TiO). Dual-Goal Gemini 0.78. Both raise I:C in 18 of 22 cases.
limits: Gains significant for thinking models; for non-thinking models mixed (small gain with TiO, small drop with Dual-Goal). Dual-Goal hurt Qwen3-14B non-thinking (0.23 to 0.13).
agent_relevance: Counterexample prompts work mainly on models that think. Use the TiO form: pick one property of the last test and flip it.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: thinking mode is not the same as less bias
finding: Switching on thinking mode raised success but did not consistently raise I:C. So long reasoning helps for other reasons than falsifying more.
numbers: Qwen3-8B baseline 0.06 to 0.21, Qwen3-32B 0.33 to 0.41, Qwen3-14B 0.23 to 0.34 (non-thinking to thinking). Thinking uses 1000 to 2000 tokens per turn versus about 6 to 14 non-thinking.
limits: Observational across three Qwen sizes.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a long trace falsifies. Add the explicit test step even for thinking models.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: distilling the intervention
finding: Fine-tuning on traces from the debiased setting raised success and I:C and partly transferred to the Blicket detector task.
numbers: Wason task: Qwen3-8B 0.21 to 0.35 (own TiO traces) and 0.59 (32B TiO teacher); Qwen3-32B 0.41 to 0.64. Blicket: 32B base 0.57, TiO prompt 0.86; 8B base 0.32, TiO 0.40; Wason-distilled students 0.34 to 0.38 (8B) and 0.77 (32B).
limits: Transfer is smaller than prompting in the new task. Training is outside our scheme (no training).
agent_relevance: The effect of the prompt is real and not a prompt artifact; supports putting it in the scaffold rather than training.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT
finding: A memorization-resistant Wason-style multi-turn benchmark: the best model solved only 14 of 50 hidden rules.
numbers: 50 rules, up to 30 test triples then a guess; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50 (28 percent), o1-mini 13/50, o1-preview 12/50, GPT-4o 9/50, Llama 3.1 405B 8/50; several small models 0 to 3/50. Jhaveri et al. cite this as 26 percent best; the table here gives 28 percent.
limits: N=50 only; the two papers disagree slightly on the top figure. Preprint (ICLR 2025 submission).
agent_relevance: Confirms the Wason failure is general for 2024 models and not a quirk of one prompt.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT: tests matter more than guesses
finding: When a model reasons from another model's tests, results change. o1-mini paired with chatgpt-4o-latest tests guessed 19 of 50 rules, above any single model. Claude 3.5 Sonnet degraded most when its justifications were removed.
numbers: 19/50 for o1-mini with 4o tests versus 13/50 alone. 2000 random lambda functions used to estimate how much each test shrinks the hypothesis space.
limits: Small N; mixed-pair design.
agent_relevance: Quality of the test set and the reasoner can be split. A test chosen by one pass and judged by another may work better.

source: Li et al. (2025) CounterMath
finding: University-level benchmark of 1,216 statement-rationale pairs where the proof is a counterexample. Most open math models score near 30 on judging true or false, and few produce good counterexamples.
numbers: 1,216 samples from 1,274 OCR pairs. F1 (macro) around 30 for open 7B models; Qwen2.5-Math-72B 41.8; DeepSeek-R1 80.7. Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct F1 38.3, strict 30.2, loose 33.2, examples 74.2 percent.
limits: Chinese textbook source translated by GPT-4o; lexical-F1 matching; judge used for strict and loose.
agent_relevance: Models often name an example but not a valid one (large gap between Examples and Strict). Validate by running the example.

source: Li et al. (2025) CounterMath: training on counterexamples
finding: SFT on 1,025 counterexample samples lifted judgment F1 and transferred to out-of-distribution math.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct F1 38.3 to 41.1 in Table 2. Table 3 OOD: MATH 80.5 to 87.9; Olympiad 41.6 to 46.4; MMLU college math 74.0 to 80.0; AIME 2024 20.0 to 30.0 (as printed, row alignment uncertain).
limits: Small sample; Table 3 is partly garbled in text extraction. Training, outside our scheme.
agent_relevance: Counterexample practice may be a general reasoning skill, supporting use of the step. Reasoning models used many more tokens without better F1.

source: Yang et al. (2025) TestCase-Eval
finding: On 500 Codeforces problems with 100,000 human solutions, models are far worse than human experts at writing one input that breaks a given wrong solution.
numbers: 19 models. Fault exposure: Qwen3-32B 43.8 percent, Qwen3-8B 41.3, GPT-4.1 36.5, GPT-4o 31.7; human experts 93.3 percent. Fault coverage: Qwen3-32B cov@1 50.8 and cov@20 95.7; GPT-4.1 cov@1 45.3 and cov@20 80.0.
limits: Experts judged on a 20-problem sample. Wrong-answer faults easier (52.2 percent for Qwen3-32B) than TLE (21.2) or memory (22.3).
agent_relevance: Many tries (cov@20) work far better than one, so run several candidate discriminating inputs and keep the best. Reasoning models and chain of thought help.

source: Yang et al. (2025) TestCase-Eval: CoT and language
finding: Chain-of-thought beat direct output for test writing; Python solutions were easier to break than C++ or Java.
numbers: Reasoning models (Qwen3) lead both tasks; CoT significantly above direct output (Figure 2). WA faults exposed at 42.0 to 52.2 percent; RE 29 to 39; TLE 16 to 23.
limits: Effect sizes shown in a figure, not read in text.
agent_relevance: Let the counterexample step reason before giving the input.

source: Prasad et al. (2025) UTGen
finding: There is a trade-off: tests that break the faulty code are hard cases, and the model gets their expected output wrong more often. Training a joint generator narrows the trade-off.
numbers: MBPP+Fix (Hard), Qwen2.5-7B: random UT attack rate 26.3, output accuracy 57.3; prompted 39.8 and 40.8; UTGen 42.0 and 58.0, combined 20.2 vs 14.7. Qwen2.5-32B: prompted 52.0 / 48.4; UTGen 56.1 / 59.2. UTDebug gains: +3.17 percent on HumanEvalFix, +12.35 percent on hard MBPP+ (Qwen2.5-32B); +13.8 percent for GPT-4o feedback.
limits: Fine-tuned generator; relies on test-time compute for output prediction.
agent_relevance: A discriminating input is only useful if we know the correct output. Get the output by running the candidate rules, not by predicting it.

source: Huang et al. (2025) POPPER
finding: An agent that designs falsification tests with sequential e-value control keeps false positives low and has higher power than LLM baselines that do not control error.
numbers: Alpha 0.1. DiscoveryBench type I: ReAct 0.145, Self-Refine 0.248, POPPER 0.152. Among controlled methods POPPER power on DiscoveryBench is 66.5 percent above ReAct; on TargetVal-IL2 3.17 times Self-Refine. Without the relevance checker type I error rises. Nine bioinformaticians as human comparison: similar quality at about 10 times less time.
limits: Statistical hypotheses on datasets, not logic claims. Some baselines exceed alpha.
agent_relevance: Falsification by LLM agents without an error gate over-confirms. Keep an irrelevant-test check and a stopping rule.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them
finding: Models are bad at finding which step is wrong but fine at fixing it when told where. So the weak link is spotting the failure.
numbers: GPT-4 best mistake finding 52.87 percent overall; logical deduction: GPT-4 40.67 percent. Backtracking with oracle mistake location raised answer accuracy by +18 to +44 points on incorrect-trace tasks (for example +43.92 multistep arithmetic).
limits: Five BIG-Bench tasks with CoT traces from PaLM 2.
agent_relevance: Counterexample search is the missing mistake-finding step. Code that locates the failing input hands the model the location.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking the model to review its own answer lowers accuracy. With a correct-label oracle it rises a lot.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7 after two rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0. Oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5.
limits: Some effect depends on prompt; they argue earlier gains used oracle labels.
agent_relevance: A counterexample check must come from a run, not from the model's opinion of its own work (G10).

source: Gu et al. (2024) The Counterfeit Conundrum
finding: Code models mistake plausible wrong programs for correct ones, predict their output as if correct, and repair them less often than they write fresh.
numbers: Correctness checking about 60 percent against 50 percent chance on two datasets; GPT-4 execution prediction near 80 percent, wrong about 20 percent.
limits: Only abstract and a few result lines read.
agent_relevance: Reading a candidate and judging it is near chance. Execute it on an input.

source: Trebacz et al. (2024) LLM Critics Help Catch LLM Bugs (CriticGPT)
finding: A trained critic finds more real bugs than paid human reviewers, but invents some. Human plus critic teams invent fewer.
numbers: Critiques preferred over human ones in 63 percent of naturally occurring LLM bug cases; critic caught more inserted bugs than contractors.
limits: Needs RLHF-trained model; hallucinated bugs can mislead.
agent_relevance: A counterexample must be executable evidence to avoid false alarms from nitpicks.

source: Eisape et al. (2023) A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models
finding: Larger PaLM 2 models reason more logically than smaller ones and than humans but copy some human biases. In the mReasoner fit, a parameter for reconsidering and searching for counterexamples (SYSTM2) tracks larger models.
numbers: Larger models reason more deliberatively (higher SYSTM2); 923 mReasoner instantiations finished simulations. Humans mostly wrongly conclude 'no artists are chemists' from a classic syllogism.
limits: Results not read in detail; fitted theory, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: Counterexample search is a tunable amount, not a switch. A full counterexample hunt costs time.

source: McCune (2003) Mace4 Reference Manual and Guide
finding: Mace4 searches for finite models of first-order formulas, giving a countermodel to a conjecture when the prover cannot show it. It builds all ground instances for one domain size, then runs a ground equational decision procedure with the least-number heuristic, and iterates upward in domain size.
numbers: Default start domain size 2; iterates size by size. Earlier Mace2 reduced to SAT but the flattening step blows up; Mace4 skips that and does better on equational problems.
limits: Finite models only; first-order satisfiability is not even semi-decidable. No benchmark numbers in the text read.
agent_relevance: The classical recipe: small cases first, then growth. Mirrors checking the smallest and weirdest inputs before large ones.

source: Blanchette (2024) Nitpick user's guide for Isabelle/HOL
finding: Nitpick finds counterexamples to higher-order claims through Kodkod and a SAT solver (MiniSat). It tries successive scopes. With infinite types it can return a potentially spurious counterexample.
numbers: Enumerates cardinalities 1 to 10 for nat by default; uses a three-valued logic for infinite types; warns when the conjecture 'either trivially holds for the given scopes or lies outside' the fragment.
limits: Not a proof of truth when none is found: it only checked small scopes.
agent_relevance: No counterexample found is weak evidence. Report the scope searched, never 'verified'. Also check a found counterexample is genuine.

source: Nickerson (1998) Confirmation bias: a ubiquitous phenomenon in many guises
finding: Review of the 2-4-6 results and the debate. People test the rule they hold with cases that fit it, so a wrong-too-narrow hypothesis is never refuted. Wetherick (1962) argued intentions were not shown; Wason replied that many still stick to hypotheses with tenacity.
numbers: Wason (1968/77) conclusion on adherence to hypotheses.
quote: even intelligent individuals adhere to their own hypotheses with remarkable tenacity
limits: Narrative review; few exact counts for 2-4-6 in this paper.
agent_relevance: Same failure the agent will have: choosing a confirming test. Needs a forced opposite test.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) positive test strategy, as reviewed by Nickerson (1998)
finding: Positive testing is not itself an error. It reveals a wrong rule when the true rule is narrower than the hypothesis, and fails when the hypothesis is the narrower. People over-rely on it as a default.
numbers: Case analysis of subset, superset, overlap, disjoint and identical rule sets; effect depends on base rates. DAX and MED labels variant improved success (secondary source).
limits: Read through Nickerson and Wikipedia, not the original paper (could not download).
agent_relevance: Rule: when the leading rule is narrower than the data allow, a confirming test is useless; test outside it. Pick tests that differ between rules.

source: Evans (1989) Bias in human reasoning, as reviewed by Nickerson (1998)
finding: Rival account: people confirm because they do not think of how to falsify, a cognitive failure of attention to positive information, not a wish to confirm. Instruction to seek disconfirmation sometimes changed behaviour but more often did not help.
numbers: Behaviour changed sometimes; performance improved less often.
limits: Second-hand report.
agent_relevance: Telling the agent to falsify may not be enough; give it a procedure (flip one property).

source: Mynatt, Doherty and Tweney (1978) via Wikipedia Confirmation bias
finding: In a long computer-simulated rule discovery task no participant found the rules over about ten hours, mostly trying to confirm; instruction in hypothesis testing had almost no effect.
numbers: None of the participants found the rules in the ten-hour session.
limits: Secondary summary only; sample size not given.
agent_relevance: Strong negative result for training people to falsify; reason to put the step in the procedure.

source: Wikipedia Wason selection task (Wason 1966, 1968; Cosmides and Tooby 1992)
finding: Fewer than 10 percent of people found the correct cards in Wason's selection task; it becomes easy as a social rule (drinking age). Low success replicated in 1993.
numbers: Under 10 percent correct in the original; Evans, Newstead and Byrne replicated in 1993; Kaufman et al. 2011 tested 112 participants on 70 items.
quote: not even 10% of subjects found the correct solution
limits: Rule framing changes the task; descriptive versus deontic conditional.
agent_relevance: Framing as rule-checking (look for a violating case) makes counterexample search natural.

source: Wagner (2021) Constructions in combinatorics via neural networks
finding: A cross-entropy reinforcement method with no prior knowledge found counterexamples to several open graph theory conjectures, but not to the most famous ones.
numbers: Refuted a question of Brualdi and Cao and several adjacency and distance eigenvalue conjectures.
limits: The author notes no famous conjecture was refuted.
agent_relevance: Search with a numeric score on the claim can find counterexamples that reasoning misses; use a score, not only yes or no.

source: Charton, Ellenberg, Wagner and Williamson (2024) PatternBoost
finding: Alternating local search and a transformer trained on best constructions found a counterexample to a 30-year-old conjecture and several best-known constructions.
numbers: One conjecture open for about 30 years refuted; performance varies by problem.
limits: Needs a scoring function and compute; results vary by problem.
agent_relevance: Supports search guided by a score for the hard cases; not a thinking schema step.
